findings.title: Findings converge on D3's full-scope pass for explicit paths
findings.why_it_matters: D3 adds one mechanism: with explicit paths and an enabled project rule, a second discovery pass loads the whole configured scope as extra input, and output is then narrowed back to the named files. Seven findings from both critics land on it from different sides:
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate D3's full-scope pass for explicit paths before addressing the converging findings individually. Open questions the re-evaluation must answer: Does a hook run need the pass at all, or can the documented pre-push entry run HSL104 without filenames? If it stays, which phase builds the extra input? What identity joins the explicit set and the full-scope set, and which spelling reports? What happens to load failures and discovery errors in files nobody named? Does the rule need the extra files' bytes?
findings.chosen: A: Re-evaluate D3's full-scope pass for explicit paths before addressing the converging findings individually. Open questions the re-evaluation must answer: Does a hook run need the pass at all, or can the documented pre-push entry run HSL104 without filenames? If it stays, which phase builds the extra input? What identity joins the explicit set and the full-scope set, and which spelling reports? What happens to load failures and discovery errors in files nobody named? Does the rule need the extra files' bytes?

findings.title: D3 threads a "report-only" class of file through `run_file_phase`; the project phase could extend its own inputs instead
findings.why_it_matters: `run_file_phase` already branches per file on load failure, language, cache hit, `--debug` replay of cached errors, and stop. A file that is loaded but gets no file rules, no cache entry, no HSL900 and no `files_scanned` count adds a fourth class of file to that loop. That means four more early-continues to get right and test, a `FilePhaseResult` change, and D3's Counts row. `FilePhaseResult.project_inputs` is already the only thing the project phase reads from the file phase. A function on the project side could run the second discovery, skip files already loaded, apply `applicable_rules`, and append to each rule's input, leaving the file loop untouched. `files_scanned` would then need no special-casing.
findings.recommended: A: Leave `run_file_phase` untouched and add a project-side step, called from `run_scan`, that runs the full-scope discovery (languages from the enabled project rules only), skips files already loaded, loads the rest, applies `applicable_rules`, and appends to each rule's input.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: Path identity is unspecified for the explicit ∪ full-scope union and for mapping jscpd's names back to input records
findings.why_it_matters: The ledger says jscpd's absolute paths "must map back to input records" and that an unmapped path fails the rule, but names no key. `LoadedFile.path` is `path.absolute()`, which is unresolved and keeps `..` and symlink names. Discovery itself keys identity on the resolved path. Two failures follow:
findings.recommended: A: Deduplicate the union by discovery's resolved path, with the explicit spelling winning for reporting. Give jscpd each file's resolved path and key the jscpd-name-to-record map on it. Add build tests for `..` and an explicit symlinked file.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: Load failures and discovery errors in files nobody named fail the run
findings.why_it_matters: D3's last table row says a file that fails to load in the extra set is "reported as an error, as any load failure". Errors give a non-zero exit (cli.py:97-100). So `house-lint check a.py` fails because of an unreadable, non-regular, or over-10-MiB file elsewhere in the tree that the user never touched. The second pass's own `discovered.errors` (for example "directory symlink is not traversed") would surface the same way. The design also doesn't say what happens when the second `discover_files` raises `DiscoveryError` (git failure, the 100k-file budget) after the first pass succeeded. Today `run_scan` handles only the first pass.
findings.recommended: A: A file that fails to load in the extra set is left out of project input, with a `--debug` line. Second-pass `discovered.errors` are dropped the same way. A second-pass `DiscoveryError` becomes a project-rule error, and file-rule results still report.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: Where "report only the named files" is applied is unspecified, and the suppressed count depends on it
findings.why_it_matters: `expand_candidates` builds `related` from every location, then checks each location's pragma, counting claimed ones as suppressed, and emits the rest. D3 says only findings located in the named paths report, but not where that cut happens. Filtering after expansion leaves `suppressed_count` including pragma-claimed copies in files the run doesn't report on, and parses pragmas of unnamed files for nothing. Filtering locations before expansion would drop them from `related`, which D3 and parent D12 say lists every copy.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: With explicit paths, jscpd runs over the full scope even when no named file is in the rule's input
findings.why_it_matters: D3 triggers the second pass whenever explicit paths are given and a project rule is enabled. If every named file is outside HSL104's input (for example, all per-file-ignored for HSL104), nothing can report, yet the full scope is loaded and jscpd runs. That costs 3-12s on hassette. Today such a rule has no input and is skipped (pipeline.py:354-355). D3 would change that.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: The extra files' bytes are loaded and never used
findings.why_it_matters: jscpd reads the real files from disk (parent D9), so `LoadedFile.content` isn't passed to it. For files outside the named set, once Finding 5's filter skips their pragma checks, the bytes serve nothing: `related` needs only `relative_path` and coordinates. A hook run on one file reads and holds every in-scope file purely to satisfy `Location.file: LoadedFile` and the rule signature. The other side: a second, path-only input type would change the project-rule contract for one rule's convenience.
findings.recommended: A: Accept loading the extra files' bytes, and state in D3 that they are loaded only to satisfy the rule contract.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: A push large enough for pre-commit to split the file list runs the full-scope pass and jscpd once per batch
findings.why_it_matters: pre-commit partitions a long filename list into several invocations. Each one would run the second discovery, load the scope, and run jscpd (3-12s, 120s timeout). The critic's concurrency concern doesn't hold: the hook declares `require_serial: true`, so batches run one after another and never share an output directory at the same time. Audience assumption: a push touching enough files to exceed pre-commit's command-line partition size (on Linux, thousands of paths), which a solo repo rarely produces.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a push large enough for pre-commit to split the file list runs the full-scope pass and jscpd once per batch, serially.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: D5 describes a merged occurrence's span as "first fragment's start to last fragment's end", which is wrong for nested fragments
findings.why_it_matters: With fragments `A:1-30` and a nested `A:10-20`, the last fragment by start ends at 20, but the merged occurrence ends at 30. The probe script D1 inherits keeps `max(end)` (clusters.py `Nodes.merged`), so the ledger's wording disagrees with the measured behaviour. Columns have the same issue: the end column must come from the fragment that owns the latest end, and the start column from the one that owns the earliest start. Implemented as written, the "N lines" in the message and the editor range would be wrong.
findings.chosen: In D5 option A and line 146, replace "from the first fragment's start to the last fragment's end" with "from the earliest fragment start to the latest fragment end, each with its own column (on a tie, the smaller start column and the larger end column), matching `clusters.py`'s `max(end)` merge".

findings.title: The column base and end-column convention are left to the build, though a probe settles them
findings.why_it_matters: The ledger says jscpd's columns are "apparently 0-based" and defers the end convention. `validate_location` requires 1-based coordinates with the end not before the start, and a `ValueError` there becomes a generic internal error that ends the project phase (pipeline.py:365-369). An off-by-one would put every span one column off. The critic also asked about non-ASCII lines. Probed during synthesis with jscpd 5.4.1:
findings.chosen: In Assumed "jscpd output" and D5, replace "columns apparently 0-based" and the build-verification sentence with: "`startLoc`/`endLoc` columns are 0-based UTF-8 byte offsets, end exclusive (probed: a match ending a 17-byte line reports 17; a match after a 2-byte `é` starts at column 3). Both convert by `+1`, matching house-lint's AST spans (`analysis.statement_key`)." Keep one real-jscpd test whose expected 1-based span is written by hand, including a non-ASCII line.

findings.title: jscpd's behaviour with zero clones isn't pinned
findings.why_it_matters: The posture treats output that "doesn't parse" as a loud failure, but the ledger only records runs that found duplicates. If a clean repo produced no report, the happy path would fail loudly. Probed during synthesis: with two small unique files, jscpd 5.4.1 exits 0 and writes `jscpd-report.json` with `"duplicates": []`. It also prints "jscpd analyzed no files" and reports `statistics.total.sources` as 0 when every input falls under its size floor. So the source count is not a usable health check. Without this fact in the ledger, a builder could guess either way.
findings.chosen: Add to Assumed "jscpd output": "With no clones, jscpd exits 0 and still writes `jscpd-report.json` with an empty `duplicates` list. `statistics.total.sources` can be 0 for inputs under its size floor, so it is not a health check. A missing report after exit 0 is a failure." Add zero-clone and single-file cases to D7's real-jscpd tests.

findings.title: jscpd's output directory and working directory are unspecified
findings.why_it_matters: jscpd writes `jscpd-report.json` to "the configured output directory", but the ledger doesn't say which directory or what cwd jscpd runs in. A fixed directory or the project root lets two runs overwrite each other's report (an editor run and a hook), leaves a report in the repo after a timeout, and lets the project's cwd influence the tool. An `OSError` launching the binary (for example, not executable) isn't in the posture's list, so it would surface as the generic internal error instead of naming the extra. The critic's "kill only the direct child" concern doesn't apply: `subprocess.run` kills the child on timeout, and jscpd 5.4.1 is a single native ELF binary (`jscpd-5.4.1.data/scripts/jscpd`) with no child tree. A loader failure on glibc below 2.34 exits non-zero, which the posture already covers.
findings.chosen: In Assumed "jscpd input", add: "The jscpd config and report live in a fresh `tempfile.TemporaryDirectory` per run, which is also jscpd's cwd and is removed afterwards. An `OSError` launching the binary raises `ProjectRuleFailure` naming the `duplicates` extra."

findings.title: Each finding's `related` list grows with cluster size, so large clusters produce very long text lines
findings.why_it_matters: A cluster of N occurrences yields N findings, each with N-1 related locations, and the text reporter appends all of them to one line. At floor 30, hassette has a 21-copy cluster (G39, bus.py docstrings) and a 16-copy one (G32 at floor 40). G39 alone prints 21 lines, each listing 20 locations. Spec 011 D4 weighed only "a 10-copy cluster". JSON consumers are unaffected beyond size.
findings.recommended: B: Keep spec 011 D4's rendering for this change.
findings.chosen: A: Cap the text reporter's `(also at ...)` suffix at a fixed number of locations, followed by "and N more"; JSON keeps every location.

findings.title: A thin overlap between fragments in one file can chain unrelated clusters and inflate the copy count
findings.why_it_matters: D1 A merges any overlapping fragments in a file, and the probe merge treats sharing even one line as overlap (`s <= merged[-1][1]`). If `A:1-30` (shared with B) and `A:30-50` (shared with C) touch on line 30, they become `A:1-50`, B and C join one cluster, and the message says "duplicated block of 50 lines, 3 copies" though no three copies share that code. The cluster may cross `min_occurrences` only because of the merge. On the other side, D1 was ratified knowing that chaining can happen, and a minimum-overlap rule reintroduces double-counting of the overlapping lines.
findings.recommended: B: Keep D1's ratified merge on any overlap.
findings.chosen: B: Keep D1's ratified merge on any overlap.
findings.choice_reason: Asked to test chaining on hassette first; the stricter merge dropped 3 of 12 real sample groups and no false ones

findings.title: `min_lines` became a config option with no evidence a project needs to turn it
findings.why_it_matters: D4's own table says `min_lines` "mostly duplicates the token floor" and "the probes never varied it". The tuning pass held it at 5. A third documented, bounded option is permanent surface (docs, validation, tests), and adding it later would be additive. On the other side, the user ratified it to let a project tune both of jscpd's size floors. At the new 30-token default, a 5-line floor may be the filter that actually binds on short Python matches. That is unmeasured either way.
findings.recommended: A: Keep `min_lines` as D4 ratified.
findings.chosen: A: Keep `min_lines` as D4 ratified.
findings.choice_reason: Asked to test it first; at 30 tokens moving min_lines 5->8 cuts pairs 58%

findings.title: D4's Bounds paragraph omits `min_lines`
findings.why_it_matters: D4's Ratified line adds `min_lines` "bounded ≥ 1 with an upper limit". The "Bounds:" paragraph a builder will copy names only `min_occurrences` and `min_tokens`. The Recommendation still saying A ("`min_lines` stays at jscpd's default") is the ledger's normal record of a recommendation the user overrode, not a contradiction. The critic's cache sub-point is already settled by code: `hash_effective_config` hashes every rule's options by design, so a changed HSL104 option re-keys file-phase entries once. That is a deliberate, cheap trade-off and needs no ledger change.
findings.chosen: Extend D4's Bounds paragraph: "`min_lines` ≥ 1, with an upper bound in the same style."

findings.title: The `min_tokens` default rests on 15 samples per floor from one repo, classified by one agent
findings.why_it_matters: D8's default rests on 12/15 against 6/15. With n=15 the interval around 80% is wide; its lower end falls below the two-thirds bar. The pooled groups overlap across floors (G05 appears at both 30 and 40), one agent classified everything, and the "real" class is mostly test setup in a test-heavy repo. The default may not carry over to a project with a different shape. D8 followed parent D17's ratified method and is easy to reverse, so this is mostly about what the docs claim.
findings.recommended: A: Add a sentence to `docs/rules.md` saying the 30-token default was tuned on hassette (15 sampled groups per floor) and that test-light projects may want to raise it.
findings.chosen: C: Leave the docs as planned.

findings.title: The docs recommend a pre-push entry with no baseline, so every push touching a file in the existing backlog fails
findings.why_it_matters: hassette has 150 groups of 3+ at the default floor. A pragma hides only its own occurrence (parent D13), so a 21-copy cluster can need 21 pragmas. With the documented pre-push entry, any push touching a file with a finding fails until it's fixed or suppressed, which happens on almost every push to hassette until `--base` (#52) exists. D8's Ratified line accepts the backlog, and parent D10 ratified the pre-push guidance. The open question is whether the docs warn about this.
findings.recommended: A: Add a docs caveat: on a repo with an existing backlog, run HSL104 by hand or in CI until it's cleared or `--base` (#52) lands, then add the pre-push entry.
findings.chosen: B: Keep the pre-push guidance as ratified, with no caveat.
findings.choice_reason: i won't release this version until 52 lands, so this should be fine, no caveat

findings.title: `jscpd==5.4.1` in the `dev` group can break `uv sync` on Mac or musl because of a missing wheel
"M copies" counts merged regions, so a chain of overlaps can report a triplicate that doesn't exist
findings.why_it_matters: Line-only overlap merging can join two different blocks, so "M copies" of one block can be false.
findings.recommended: A: Reword the message and `docs/rules.md` to count locations rather than copies of one block (for example `duplicated code of 30-60 lines in 3 places`)
findings.chosen: A: Reword the message and `docs/rules.md` to count locations rather than copies of one block (for example `duplicated code of 30-60 lines in 3 places`)

findings.title: Enabling HSL104 in config breaks the commit-stage hook, and the docs only describe the CLI route
findings.why_it_matters: Config selection also runs HSL104 in the commit-stage hook, which has no jscpd.
findings.chosen: Add a sentence telling users to enable HSL104 with --select in the pre-push hook, not extend-select in config

findings.title: Timeout and crash failures tell the user to reinstall jscpd
findings.why_it_matters: After the version check passes, the install hint points the wrong way.
findings.recommended: A: Drop the install hint from the analysis run's timeout and non-zero-exit messages; the timeout says the limit is fixed and how many files were given. Keep the hint for a missing binary, a wrong version, a version check that fails to run, a missing or unreadable report, and an unknown name.
findings.chosen: A: Drop the install hint from the analysis run's timeout and non-zero-exit messages; the timeout says the limit is fixed and how many files were given. Keep the hint for a missing binary, a wrong version, a version check that fails to run, a missing or unreadable report, and an unknown name.

findings.title: The jscpd config keys behind documented behaviour have no test that would fail without them
findings.why_it_matters: Removing mode weak or gitignore false would leave every test green.
findings.recommended: A: Add a test whose copies differ only in comments (expects a match), and run the `.jscpd.json`/`.gitignore` test once with `-c` and `"gitignore": False` removed; if it still passes, rewrite it so it fails without them
findings.chosen: A: Add a test whose copies differ only in comments (expects a match), and run the `.jscpd.json`/`.gitignore` test once with `-c` and `"gitignore": False` removed; if it still passes, rewrite it so it fails without them

findings.title: Nothing checks that jscpd analyzed every file it was given
findings.why_it_matters: A file jscpd silently skips drops out of HSL104 with no error.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation
findings.chosen: A: Fail on any non-Python format + `--debug` count
findings.choice_reason: User walked it individually after past silent-skip trouble; probes showed per-format counts exist, and the pre-commit review replaced the format check with a .py suffix pre-check that covers unknown suffixes too.

findings.title: The 120-second timeout is fixed, so a scope that outgrows it can only disable the rule
findings.why_it_matters: A scope over 120s has no knob short of disabling HSL104.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation

findings.title: The version check runs with the full 120-second timeout
findings.why_it_matters: A wedged binary could stall a hook up to 240s.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation
findings.chosen: A: Give the version check its own short timeout
findings.choice_reason: User agreed it is a code-shape smell with a cheap fix.

findings.title: jscpd re-reads files from disk, so a file edited mid-run can put a span where its pragmas don't claim it
findings.why_it_matters: A mid-run edit can misplace one run's finding.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation

findings.why_it_matters: Very low floors on a huge repo could exhaust memory.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation

findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation

findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation

A file reached under two spellings is deduplicated to the first, so the second named spelling gets no finding
